idiom_name: function-local static with guaranteed thread-safe initialisation
implementation_notes: The language absorbed the pattern: since C++11 a block-scope static is initialised the first time control passes through its declaration and, if several threads reach it concurrently, the initialisation occurs exactly once - cppreference states the guarantee explicitly, so the classic marker test disappears and the accessor becomes 'static Foo f; return f;'. The same mechanism gives lazily built singletons (Meyers form) and lazily created shared dependencies, with no lock on the fast path after initialisation. A throwing initialiser leaves the static uninitialised, so the initialisation is attempted again on the next traversal.
pitfalls: Thread safety applies to block-scope statics only: a namespace-scope or member static is initialised before main, which is how the static-initialisation-order fiasco (and the construct-on-first-use idiom) arise.

MSVC before 2015 did not implement magic statics, and code that wraps the static in a hand-written double-checked fast path (a raw pointer test outside the static) is still a data race on any standard library.

A recursive initialiser (the static's constructor using the accessor) is undefined/deadlocking rather than merely slow, and destroying a function-local static at exit can race with other threads' use during shutdown.

variants.name: std::call_once over a std::once_flag
variants.implementation_notes: When the initialisation is not tied to one variable - registering handlers, warming a global registry, applying a one-time configuration - std::call_once(f, fn) with a std::once_flag is the library form of the same guarantee. Unlike the static-local form, a throwing callable neither completes nor poisons the flag: cppreference documents that the exception is propagated and the flag is not flipped, so the next call attempts the initialisation again - a retry-friendly, but also potentially repeated, failure policy.
pitfalls: std::call_once blocks every concurrent caller until the callable returns, and if the callable throws, the flag is not flipped: repeated failures mean repeated blocking and repeated side effects, so the callable should be exception-safe.
once_flag is neither copyable nor movable and must outlive every caller; a once_flag in a destroyed object leaves callers with a dangling flag.
The callable returning void means success/failure must be encoded in the shared state it writes, not in its return value.

variants.name: Resettable lazy cell (std::optional plus mutex/atomic)
variants.idiom_name: std::optional<T> cell guarded by std::mutex (or atomic publication)
variants.implementation_notes: When the value must be rebuildable (configuration reload, connection loss) the once-forms are the wrong tool because they can never run the initialiser a second time; the replacement is an explicit cell - std::optional<T> plus a std::mutex, or, for a hot read path, an std::atomic flag with release publication and a pointer/shared_ptr payload. It trades the language guarantee for a reset operation and a hand-written publication protocol, which is exactly why it should be the exception.
pitfalls: The lock is now taken on every access, not only on the first, so a resettable cell is a different performance bargain than a function-local static.
Hand-rolled atomic publication must use acquire/release (or a mutex); a plain pointer test plus a non-atomic store reproduces the pre-C++11 double-checked locking bug.

Invalidation races are the point of this variant and are the responsibility of the owner: a reader may hold a reference to the old value while another thread resets the cell (use shared_ptr snapshots if that is possible).
